title: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
hookLine: even in war, fruit trees are spared; the rabbis made it a ban on all waste

lines: A CITY WON'T OPEN ITS GATES.
AN ARMY STOPS AT THE EDGE.
cards: A city won't open its gates. The army camped outside has axes, and all around the walls stand orchards. Olive trees, fig trees, date palms that took years to grow.
Cut them down, and you get timber for siege works, and you break the people inside: hungry now, and poorer for years after. In war, the usual limits tend to fall away.
And right in the middle of the Torah's laws of war, there's a verse that stops an army at the edge of an orchard.

teach.h: DON'T TAKE THE AXE TO THE TREES.
teach.b: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: when you besiege a city a long time, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by wielding an axe against them." You may eat from them. You may not cut them down.
Then a question: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?" The tree isn't your enemy. It can't run behind the walls.

The Hebrew can also be read as a statement: for man is a tree of the field. The medieval commentator Ibn Ezra reads it that way: people live from trees, so destroying them destroys your own life. Two readings, one point.
From the words thou shalt not destroy, lo tashchit, the rabbis built a whole principle, called bal tashchit: do not destroy needlessly. And they took it far beyond orchards and war.
Maimonides writes that anyone who smashes dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, blocks a spring or wastes food destructively breaks this law.
In the Talmud, one rabbi goes further: someone who could eat barley bread but eats the costlier wheat bread has broken it.
Others there push back that caring for your own body comes first, but the reach of the idea is clear.

teach.h: IF IN WAR, HOW MUCH MORE IN PEACE.
teach.b: If even in war, when everything feels permitted, you can't destroy a tree for no reason, then in peacetime, in your own kitchen, how much more.
In this tradition, waste is a kind of small destruction.

how: Bal tashchit is a recognized principle of Jewish law, applied to waste of food, objects, energy and resources, and Jewish environmental teaching often begins from this verse about the fruit trees.

o: do not covet: the rule against wanting more
do not steal: the rule against taking property
do not destroy: the rule against needless waste

games.q: inside bal tashchit — tap the pairs.
p: man is a tree of the field

s: the verse forbids eating from the enemy's trees
you may eat from them; you may not cut them down.
the rabbis applied bal tashchit to food, clothes and buildings
Maimonides lists smashing dishes, tearing clothes, wasting food.
the Hebrew can be read as a question or as a statement
is the tree a man? or, man is a tree of the field.

games.q: your army is besieging a city that won't surrender. the orchards around it would make good siege timber. what does the Torah say?
o: cut them down to break the city.
eat from them, but don't cut them down.
burn them so the enemy can't use them.
games.why: thou mayest eat of them, but thou shalt not cut them down. is the tree of the field a man, to be besieged?

practice: Picture your day in things: the food in the fridge close to turning, the lights on in empty rooms, the shirt waiting on one loose button.
Pick one, and picture the small act that saves it, eating the leftovers, flipping the switch, sewing the button. Each one is tiny, and each one is a tree left standing.

wordCard.voice: Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. The rabbis' rule against needless destruction and waste, drawn from the fruit trees of Shoftim.

orig.note: Hebrew: do not destroy. the rabbis' principle against waste, from lo tashchit in Deuteronomy 20:19.

carryVoice: Your line: don't destroy needlessly. If a tree is spared in war, how much more a meal at home. Day five hundred five, done.
